Well, Doc... I guess I'm here because I did something recently that really just didn't sit right with me. 

You see, I run a fairly large company. Built it from the ground up, actually. Never have. It's been eating at me all week, honestly, because I just don't know where that kind of reaction came from. I can't be flying off the handle over a warehouse heating bill when hundreds of people are relying on me to steer the ship, you know? It really rattled me.

No, no, never. That’s exactly why I’m sitting in this chair right now, Doc. If I was the kind of guy who just went around yelling at people all the time, I probably wouldn’t have thought twice about it, right? I mean, there are plenty of bosses out there like that. And for thirty-something years, I really have been.

Millions of dollars on the line, and I just rolled up my sleeves, got everybody a cup of coffee, and said, 'Alright, how do we fix this?' That's how you handle things. 

So, no... I've never snapped like that before. Usually, if a guy messes up a budget line, I pull him aside later, we look at the spreadsheet together, and we figure it out. For me to just bark at him like a junkyard dog right there on a conference call... it was completely out of left field. Just this one time, just out of the blue, over a heating bill of all things. Anxious? On edge? Yeah... yeah, Doc, I'd say that hits the nail right on the head. It's like my whole body is just wound up tight, like one of those cheap pocket watches you overwind and you can just feel the gears straining, you know?

Thoughts? Yeah... yeah, I guess you could call them that. But it feels more like... well, it’s like a bad film that I didn't ask to see, you know? A movie somebody just forces you to watch when you're trying to do something else. 

I'll be sitting there, just doing the mundane stuff I've done ten thousand times to keep this company running. And then, out of nowhere, the blast and that fire by the loading area just jump back into my head. 

Just... boom. Right there behind my eyes. It's not even like I'm trying to remember it. I'm actively trying *not* to. But I can see the flames going up the side of the corrugated metal, I can see the whole mess at the loading dock, and it completely derails me. One second I'm looking at a spreadsheet or talking about freight costs, and the next I'm just staring blankly at the wall, seeing that fire all over again. 

I have to literally shake my head, like a dog shaking off water, just to get back to reality. And the guys on the phone, they'll be sitting there saying, 'Boss? You still there? We lose you?' And I have to clear my throat and pretend I was just reviewing a file or reading an email. But really, my mind was miles away, stuck right back at that loading area watching it burn. It just plays on a loop, Doc. I can't seem to shut the projector off, no matter how hard I try to focus on the work in front of me.

Specific thoughts or memories I'm trying to avoid? Well... no. Not really. I mean, I know I just spent ten minutes telling you how I can't drive past the new building or open those safety files, but that's different. That's stuff out there in the world. But my own thoughts? No, I'm not really doing that.

I actually dropped out of school halfway through the eighth grade. Eighth grade! Most kids my age were complaining about homework or whatever, and I was out hauling scrap metal and sweeping warehouse floors for fifty cents an hour just to help my old man pay the heating bill. When you grow up like that, and you build a company like mine from absolute scratch, you learn pretty quick that you can't run away from what's in your head. If there's a problem, you look at it. You figure it out. You don't get to be the boss by burying your head in the sand every time you remember a bad day.

So, no, I'm not sitting around trying to block out specific memories of the... the incident. It's not like I'm sitting in my office saying, 'Oh, don't think about the smoke,' or 'Don't think about the sirens.' I'm not doing that. Like I said before, the memories just sort of pop up on their own, like a bad movie playing in the background while I'm trying to look at my spreadsheets. But I'm not actively trying to shove the thoughts away or dodge certain parts of what happened. I just... I just want to get my work done, you know? I've got three hundred employees relying on me to make payroll next Friday, so I don't have the luxury of sitting around playing hide-and-seek with my own memories. If the thought comes, it comes. I just grit my teeth, take a breath, and try to look back down at the balance sheet. So no, I wouldn't say I'm trying to avoid any specific thoughts about it.

I've never snapped like that before. Usually, if a guy messes up a budget line, I pull him aside later, we look at the spreadsheet together, and we figure it out. For me to just bark at him like a junkyard dog right there on a conference call... it was completely out of left field. Just this one time, just out of the blue, over a heating bill of all things. It hasn't happened since, and it's never happened before. Just this one single incident, and it completely threw me because it's just... it's just not who I am.\n\nDoctor: Has this incident affected your relationships with your employees or your ability to perform your job duties since it happened?\n\nPatient: Well, that's the thing, Doc. I haven't missed a day of work. But... am I really doing my job? That's the question I've been wrestling with all week. \n\nBecause ever since that call, I've just been... second-guessing myself. I kept thinking, 'What if I miss something? What if I misread the budget and snap at somebody again?' So I put it off. I told them we'd revisit it next week. And then yesterday, there was a vendor dispute I would usually mediate myself, just get both guys on the phone and hash it out. Instead, I handed it off to my VP of Operations. I just told him, 'You handle this one, I've got too much on my plate.' Which wasn't true. I just didn't trust myself to get on that call and stay level-headed. \n\nAnd my employees... they're professionals, they're not going to say anything to my face. But I can see it. Well, connecting... I mean, I'm still around them, you know? I haven't locked myself in the basement or anything. I'm still showing up. But it’s... it’s different. I mentioned my wife earlier, right? If my people are afraid to bring me a problem, then the company is in danger. \n\nSo yeah, I'm technically still at the helm, but... I'm leaning heavily on my executive team for things I should be doing myself. I'm delaying calls, I'm avoiding decisions about the facilities, and it's all because that one blow-up made me realize that whatever is going on with me right now, it's starting to affect my judgment. And as a CEO, if you can't trust your own judgment, you've got nothing. So it's definitely impacting how I'm running things, even if the bottom line hasn't shown it yet. I just can't have my people walking on eggshells around me, Doc. It's not right.\n\nDoctor: Have you been feeling anxious or on edge most of the time since the incident?\n\nPatient: Anxious? On edge? Yeah... yeah, Doc, I'd say that hits the nail right on the head. But I just can't settle into the chair. My shoulders are practically up to my ears all day. I jump like something went off again. Just this massive jolt right through my chest, like a shock of electricity. I grew up around forklifts dropping heavy pallets, delivery trucks backing up, metal clanging against metal on the loading docks... none of that ever bothered me. I could sleep through a freight train going by. But now? A door clicks shut a little too loud and I'm sitting there vibrating for five minutes trying to catch my breath. I've never felt anything like it.\n\nDoctor: Have you been having any recurring, intrusive thoughts since the incident?\n\nPatient: Thoughts? Yeah... yeah, I guess you could call them that. Guilty? Yeah. Yeah, Doc, I do. Honestly, it’s eating at me. I mean, that’s... that’s the whole reason I’m sitting in this chair talking to you today. I came in because I snapped on that board call, and I mean, I really snapped.
